items.prompt: Two functions both finish in 2ms on a 200-row test file. What does that tell you about their Big-O complexity?
choices: They must have the same Big-O complexity, since they take the same time
Almost nothing — Big-O describes how work grows as input size grows, not the runtime on one specific input size
The faster one at 200 rows will always stay faster at any input size
Big-O only applies to functions that take more than 1 second to run
items.explanation: Big-O describes a growth RATE, not a single measurement. Two functions can tie at small n and diverge enormously at large n — which is exactly what the unit's incident demonstrated.
items.reference:
n=200: O(n) and O(n²) both finish instantly

n=500,000: O(n) = 500K units of work; O(n²) = 250 BILLION

Why: a single timing on one input size can't reveal a growth rate.
items.learnMore:
Growth rate vs. one measurement

A stopwatch reading tells you about ONE input size. Big-O tells you the SHAPE of the curve as input size changes — the only way to actually distinguish two complexity classes is to measure (or reason about) multiple, growing input sizes.

Common mistake

Concluding 'it's fast' from one test run on a small fixture, the exact mistake that shipped the unit's incident.

No, because Big-O only applies to inputs larger than 1,000

items.prompt: A 200-row CI fixture can't reveal an O(n²) bug that only causes real problems at 500,000 rows. Why not?

It's impossible to write a test that would ever catch this class of bug
items.explanation: At small n, the absolute difference between O(n) and O(n²) work is tiny in real time, even though the RATIO is already large — the gap only becomes painfully visible once n is big enough for the multiplicative difference to translate into seconds or minutes.

items.learnMore:
Why small fixtures lie

A test fixture proves correctness, not scalability. The only way to catch a growth-rate problem in CI is to deliberately test with an input size close to production scale, or to review the code for the nested-scan pattern directly.

Common mistake

Assuming 'passes CI' means 'safe at production scale' — CI fixtures are usually sized for speed, not for realism.

items.prompt: Which of these is a classic example of O(log n) — logarithmic complexity?
choices: Scanning every item in an unsorted list to find a value
Binary search in a sorted array — each step eliminates half the remaining possibilities
Comparing every item to every other item
Reading a single item from an array by its index
items.explanation: Binary search halves the search space on each step, which is exactly the shape of logarithmic growth — doubling the input only adds one more step.
items.reference:
ClassExample
O(1)array[5] by index
O(log n)binary search
O(n)scan every item once
O(n²)compare every item to every other

Why: matching a pattern to its typical example is the fastest way to recognize a complexity class in real code.
items.learnMore:
Recognizing the shape

Most real-world complexity classes map to a recognizable code shape: direct index access is O(1); a single loop over the input is O(n); halving a search space each step is O(log n); a loop nested inside a loop over the same collection is O(n²).

Common mistake

Assuming 'sorted' automatically means O(log n) lookups — only true if the code actually uses a search that exploits the sort, like binary search.

items.prompt: At n=1,000,000, O(n) work is 1,000,000 units and O(log n) work is roughly 20 units. What does this gap tell you?

The two numbers are actually the same when measured correctly
O(log n) only works for arrays smaller than 1,000
items.explanation: Logarithmic growth is famously slow-growing — doubling n only adds one more unit of work, which is why algorithms with this shape (like binary search, or balanced tree operations) stay fast even at enormous scale.

items.prompt: A loop does 5 operations per item instead of 1. What's its Big-O complexity, and why doesn't the '5' appear in it?
choices: O(5n) — the 5 has to stay in the notation
O(n) — Big-O drops constant multipliers, since they become irrelevant next to how the DOMINANT term (n) grows as n approaches infinity
O(n⁵) — multiplying operations raises the power
It's impossible to express in Big-O notation
items.explanation: Constant factors (like 'doing 5 things per item' instead of 1) don't change the fundamental growth SHAPE — the function is still fundamentally O(n), just with a bigger constant. Big-O deliberately ignores that constant.
items.reference:
O(3n) → O(n)

O(n² + n) → O(n²)

Why: constants and lower-order terms become irrelevant as n grows toward infinity.
items.learnMore:
Why constants get dropped

Big-O cares about the LIMITING behavior as n grows without bound. A constant multiplier (3n vs n) changes the exact runtime but not the fundamental shape of the curve — both are straight lines, just with different slopes. That's a real, sometimes important difference in practice, but it's a different question from 'which growth class is this.'

Common mistake

Thinking Big-O is a full performance model — it deliberately discards information (constants) that can still matter for real-world tuning.

items.prompt: A function does `n² + n` operations total. What's its simplified Big-O?
choices: O(n² + n) — both terms must be kept
O(n²) — the n² term dominates completely as n grows large, making the +n term negligible by comparison
O(n) — the lower term is always kept, the higher one dropped
O(2n²) — the two terms combine multiplicatively
items.explanation: Dropping lower-order terms is one of the standard Big-O simplification rules — as n grows large, n² utterly dominates n, so the sum simplifies to just O(n²).
items.reference:

O(n² + n) → O(n²)

Why: constants and lower-order terms become irrelevant as n grows toward infinity.

items.prompt: What real-world code pattern most commonly produces O(n²) complexity by accident?
choices: A single loop that reads each item once
A loop where each iteration performs an operation (like a membership check or a search) that itself scans the whole collection
A function with a long list of if/else statements
Recursion with no base case
items.explanation: A loop of n iterations where each iteration does O(n) work (like scanning an array for membership) multiplies to O(n²) — this is exactly the shape of the unit's incident, disguised as a single innocent-looking check.
items.reference:
for record in records: # n times
  if record.id not in result: # scans up to n items

Why: n outer iterations × up to n inner scan work = O(n²) — no visible nested `for` keyword required.
items.learnMore:
The disguised nested loop

Array methods like `.includes()`, `.indexOf()`, and `.find()` are themselves O(n) operations — calling one inside a loop over the same collection is functionally a nested loop, even though the code only shows one explicit `for`.

Common mistake

Scanning code for a literal nested `for` loop and concluding 'no nested loop, so it can't be O(n²)' — the scan can be hidden inside a single method call.

`.includes()` is always O(1), so this code is actually O(n)
Only recursive functions can be O(n²)

items.prompt: Before shipping code that processes a growing collection, what question does this unit recommend asking — beyond 'does it pass on my test data'?
choices: "Does the code compile without warnings?"
"What happens to the amount of work if n were 1,000x bigger than my test data?"

"Did a senior engineer review this line by line?"
items.explanation: This is the unit's core practical question — it directly targets growth rate, which passing tests on small data can't reveal at all.
items.reference:
Ask before shipping: "what happens to the work if n were 1,000x bigger?"

Why: this question targets growth rate directly, which passing tests on small data never reveals.
items.learnMore:
A habit, not a formula

Most engineers don't formally derive Big-O for every function they write — the practical version of this skill is a habit: glance at any loop processing a collection and ask whether anything inside it also scales with the collection's size.

Common mistake

Treating complexity analysis as an academic exercise reserved for interviews, rather than a five-second sanity check before merging.

items.prompt: In the incident's original code, what specifically makes `record.id not in result` an O(n) operation rather than O(1)?
choices: Because `result` is a plain list/array — checking membership means scanning items one by one until a match is found or the list ends
Because Python and JavaScript always make membership checks O(n) regardless of data structure
Because `record.id` is a string instead of a number
It's actually O(1) — the analysis in this unit is wrong
items.explanation: The O(n) cost comes specifically from the underlying data structure — a plain list has no shortcut for membership checking, so it must scan. A different data structure (a Set/hash) changes this without changing the surrounding loop at all.
items.reference:
for record in records: # n times
  if record.id not in result: # scans up to n items EVERY time

Why: the outer loop runs n times; each iteration's check can itself scan up to n items.
items.learnMore:
The data structure IS the complexity

The same logical operation ('have I seen this id before?') has a completely different Big-O cost depending on what it's checked against — O(n) against a list, O(1) average-case against a Set. This is why the fix in L2/L3 changes a data structure, not the loop's logic.

Common mistake

Trying to optimize the outer loop's logic when the actual cost lives in the inner membership check's data structure.

items.prompt: Why is a `Set`'s `.has()` check O(1) on average, while an array's `.includes()` is O(n)?
choices: Sets are just faster arrays under the hood, with no structural difference
A Set (hash-based) computes a hash of the value and jumps almost directly to the right storage bucket, instead of scanning every stored item one by one like an array must
Sets can only hold numbers, which makes comparisons faster
There's no real difference — this is a common misconception
items.explanation: A hash-based Set uses the value's hash to jump nearly straight to its bucket, avoiding a linear scan entirely — this structural difference, not raw speed, is what makes the average-case complexity O(1) instead of O(n).
items.reference:
StructureMembership check
Array/listO(n) — scan until found or end
Set/hashO(1) average — hash jumps to bucket

Why: swapping the data structure — not adding cleverness to the loop — is what collapses the complexity.
items.learnMore:
Hashing in one sentence

A hash function converts a value into a number used as an index into internal storage — so 'is this value present' becomes 'look at approximately one specific slot' instead of 'check every slot,' which is the mechanical reason the average case is O(1).

Common mistake

Assuming Sets are fast because they're a 'newer' or 'more optimized' data type in general, rather than because of this specific structural property.

items.prompt: A function performs 3 array scans of length n, one after another (not nested). What's its Big-O?
choices: O(n³) — three scans multiply
O(3n), which simplifies to O(n) — sequential (non-nested) operations ADD, and constant multipliers are dropped
O(n) — but only because 3 is a small number
It cannot be determined without running it
items.explanation: Sequential operations add rather than multiply: n + n + n = 3n. Dropping the constant factor per the standard simplification rule gives O(n) — multiplying would only apply if the scans were NESTED, not sequential.
items.reference:
Nested loops multiply: O(n) × O(n) = O(n²)

Sequential steps add, largest wins: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n)

Why: whether operations are nested or sequential completely changes how their costs combine.
items.learnMore:
Nested vs. sequential is the whole ballgame

The single biggest source of Big-O confusion in real code is mixing up 'this loop happens inside that loop' (multiply) with 'this loop happens, then separately that loop happens' (add). Reading the code structure carefully — indentation, not just presence of `for` — is what tells them apart.

Common mistake

Seeing multiple loops in a function and assuming they must multiply, without checking whether they're nested or sequential.

Seeing multiple loops in a function and assuming they must multiply, without checking whether they're nested or sequential.

items.prompt: A function does an O(n) pass, then a separate O(n²) pass over the same data afterward (not nested). What's the overall complexity?
choices: O(n) — the smaller pass is what matters
O(n³) — the passes multiply
O(n²) — sequential steps add, and n² dominates n as the larger term
It's impossible to combine two passes over the same array
items.explanation: Sequential steps add: O(n) + O(n²). Since n² dominates n for large inputs, the combined complexity simplifies to O(n²) — the larger of the two sequential terms.
items.reference:
Nested loops multiply: O(n) × O(n) = O(n²)

Sequential steps add, largest wins: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n)

Why: whether operations are nested or sequential completely changes how their costs combine.

items.prompt: A Set's O(1) lookup is described as an 'average case' claim. What does that qualifier actually mean, and when might it not hold?
choices: It means the claim is unreliable and Sets shouldn't be trusted for performance-sensitive code
It means that under typical conditions the lookup is O(1), but in a rare worst case — many values hashing into the same bucket (collisions) — a lookup can degrade toward O(n)
It means Sets are O(1) exactly half the time and O(n) the other half
It has no real meaning — 'average case' is just a figure of speech
items.explanation: Big-O claims are often tied to a specific case (best/worst/average). A Set's O(1) is an average-case guarantee that assumes hash values spread out reasonably; heavy hash collisions (rare in practice, but possible, especially under adversarial input) can push a lookup toward O(n) in the worst case.
items.reference:
Fine print

Set/Map O(1) is an AVERAGE case claim, not a worst-case guarantee.

Why: heavy hash collisions (rare, but possible) can degrade a lookup toward O(n).
items.learnMore:
Which case is being claimed?

Big-O statements almost always describe a specific case — best, worst, or average — even when the case isn't stated explicitly. Confusing 'this is O(1) on average' with 'this is O(1), guaranteed, always' is a common source of surprise when a system behaves unexpectedly under unusual or adversarial input.

Common mistake

Citing a Big-O claim without knowing (or asking) which case — best, worst, or average — it actually describes.
